claim: Imaginal progenitors in Drosophila are known to arrest in G2 during larval stages and proliferate thereafter.
source: Imaginal progenitors in Drosophila are known to arrest in G2 during larval stages and proliferate thereafter.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Tracheoblasts pause in G2 for approximately 48-56 hours.
source: We report that tracheoblasts pause in G2 for ~48–56 h and grow in size over this period.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Tracheoblasts grow in size during G2 arrest.
source: We report that tracheoblasts pause in G2 for ~48–56 h and grow in size over this period.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Tracheoblasts arrested in G2 express Cdc25/String (Stg).
source: Surprisingly, tracheoblasts arrested in G2 express drivers of G2-M like Cdc25/String (Stg).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Tracheoblasts activate Checkpoint Kinase 1/Grapes (Chk1/Grp) in an ATR/mei-41-dependent manner.
source: Tracheoblasts activate Checkpoint Kinase 1/Grapes (Chk1/Grp) in an ATR/mei-41-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Loss of ATR/Chk1 led to precocious mitotic entry approximately 24-32 hours earlier than normal.
source: Loss of ATR/Chk1 led to precocious mitotic entry ~24–32 h earlier.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Precocious divisions in ATR/Chk1 mutants were apparently normal with no evidence of increased DNA damage or cell death.
source: These divisions were apparently normal as there was no evidence of increased DNA damage or cell death.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Induction of precocious mitoses impaired growth of tracheoblasts and the tracheae they comprise.
source: However, induction of precocious mitoses impaired growth of tracheoblasts and the tracheae they comprise.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: ATR/Chk1 negatively regulate G2-M in developing tracheoblasts.
source: We propose that ATR/Chk1 negatively regulate G2-M in developing tracheoblasts and that G2 arrest facilitates cellular and hypertrophic organ growth.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: G2 arrest facilitates cellular and hypertrophic organ growth.
source: We propose that ATR/Chk1 negatively regulate G2-M in developing tracheoblasts and that G2 arrest facilitates cellular and hypertrophic organ growth.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Non-cycling cells are known to pause in G1 (or G0).
source: Non-cycling cells are known to pause in G1 (or G0) (Cheung and Rando, 2013) or, less commonly, in the G2 phase (Bouldin and Kimelman, 2014) of the cell cycle and rekindle a mitotic program at the appropriate time and location.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Non-cycling cells less commonly pause in the G2 phase.
source: Non-cycling cells are known to pause in G1 (or G0) (Cheung and Rando, 2013) or, less commonly, in the G2 phase (Bouldin and Kimelman, 2014) of the cell cycle and rekindle a mitotic program at the appropriate time and location.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested cells have been observed in developing Drosophila.
source: G2-arrested cells have been observed in developing Drosophila (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Ayeni et al., 2016), Ciona (Ogura et al., 2011), zebrafish (Nguyen et al., 2017), chick (Boije et al., 2009; Stone et al., 1999) and mice (Seki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested cells have been observed in Ciona.
source: G2-arrested cells have been observed in developing Drosophila (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Ayeni et al., 2016), Ciona (Ogura et al., 2011), zebrafish (Nguyen et al., 2017), chick (Boije et al., 2009; Stone et al., 1999) and mice (Seki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested cells have been observed in zebrafish.
source: G2-arrested cells have been observed in developing Drosophila (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Ayeni et al., 2016), Ciona (Ogura et al., 2011), zebrafish (Nguyen et al., 2017), chick (Boije et al., 2009; Stone et al., 1999) and mice (Seki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested cells have been observed in chick.
source: G2-arrested cells have been observed in developing Drosophila (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Ayeni et al., 2016), Ciona (Ogura et al., 2011), zebrafish (Nguyen et al., 2017), chick (Boije et al., 2009; Stone et al., 1999) and mice (Seki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested cells have been observed in mice.
source: G2-arrested cells have been observed in developing Drosophila (Johnston and Edgar, 1998; Ayeni et al., 2016), Ciona (Ogura et al., 2011), zebrafish (Nguyen et al., 2017), chick (Boije et al., 2009; Stone et al., 1999) and mice (Seki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fruit flies undergo a complete metamorphosis during their life cycle and have distinct larval and adult body forms.
source: Fruit flies undergo a complete metamorphosis during their life cycle and have distinct larval and adult body forms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Progenitors of the adult animal are set aside during embryonic development, nourished in the larva, and activated during the larval-adult transition.
source: Progenitors of the adult animal (hereafter referred to as imaginal progenitors) are set aside during embryonic development, nourished in the larva, and activated during the larval-adult transition (Cohen et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Imaginal progenitors generate adult organs de novo or by remodeling larval organs.
source: These progenitors generate adult organs de novo (sensory organs, wings, legs) or by remodeling larval organs (gut, abdominal epidermis, tracheal system).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Progenitors of the abdominal epidermis (histoblasts) exhibit punctuated proliferation patterns.
source: The progenitors of the abdominal epidermis (histoblasts)(Ninov et al., 2009), and the thoracic tracheal (respiratory) system (Djabrayan et al., 2014; Guha et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2008; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008; Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010) exhibit the latter pattern.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Progenitors of the thoracic tracheal system exhibit punctuated proliferation patterns.
source: The progenitors of the abdominal epidermis (histoblasts)(Ninov et al., 2009), and the thoracic tracheal (respiratory) system (Djabrayan et al., 2014; Guha et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2008; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008; Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010) exhibit the latter pattern.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Histoblasts and thoracic tracheal progenitors remain mitotically arrested in G2 through most of larval life and initiate a program of rapid cell division and morphogenesis thereafter.
source: These cells remain mitotically arrested in G2 through most of larval life and initiate a program of rapid cell division and morphogenesis thereafter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these cell types.

claim: The mechanism for G2-M is highly conserved among eukaryotic cells.
source: The mechanism for G2-M is highly conserved among eukaryotic cells (Bouldin and Kimelman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The G2-M transition is triggered by the dephosphorylation of the Cyclin-dependent Kinase Cdc2/Cdk1 by the phosphatase Cdc25.
source: The G2-M transition is triggered by the dephosphorylation of the Cyclin-dependent Kinase Cdc2/Cdk1 by the phosphatase Cdc25.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Cdc2/Cdk1 by Cdc25 results in the activation of the Cdk-Cyclin B complex.
source: Dephosphorylation of Cdc2/Cdk1 by Cdc25 results in the activation of the Cdk-Cyclin B complex and in turn to the phosphorylation of substrates in the cytoplasm and nucleus and to mitotic entry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Activation of the Cdk-Cyclin B complex leads to phosphorylation of substrates in the cytoplasm and nucleus and to mitotic entry.
source: Dephosphorylation of Cdc2/Cdk1 by Cdc25 results in the activation of the Cdk-Cyclin B complex and in turn to the phosphorylation of substrates in the cytoplasm and nucleus and to mitotic entry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: G2-arrested progenitors of sensory organs (SOPs) in Drosophila repress Cdc25/String (Stg) expression.
source: G2-arrested progenitors of sensory organs (SOPs) in Drosophila have been shown to repress Cdc25/String (Stg) expression (Johnston and Edgar, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOPs forced to divide precociously undergo normal neuronal differentiation but generate supernumerary non-neuronal sensory organ support cells.
source: A recent study showed that SOPs forced to divide precociously undergo normal neuronal differentiation but generate supernumerary non-neuronal sensory organ support cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature (Ayeni et al., 2016 mentioned earlier in the paragraph).

claim: G2 arrest in SOPs is mediated by the transcriptional repression of Stg.
source: Taken together, studies on SOPs show that G2 arrest is mediated by the transcriptional repression of Stg and that the arrest ensures that a proper balance of cell types within each sensory organ is achieved (Ayeni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: G2 arrest in SOPs ensures that a proper balance of cell types within each sensory organ is achieved.
source: Taken together, studies on SOPs show that G2 arrest is mediated by the transcriptional repression of Stg and that the arrest ensures that a proper balance of cell types within each sensory organ is achieved (Ayeni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Non-cycling histoblasts lack Stg expression.
source: Non-cycling histoblasts lack Stg expression and upregulate Stg in an ecdysteroid signaling-dependent manner during G2-M(Ninov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Histoblasts upregulate Stg in an ecdysteroid signaling-dependent manner during G2-M.
source: Non-cycling histoblasts lack Stg expression and upregulate Stg in an ecdysteroid signaling-dependent manner during G2-M(Ninov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the sea squirt Ciona, progenitors undergoing neurulation are known to arrest in G2.
source: In the sea squirt Ciona, progenitors undergoing neurulation are known to arrest in G2 (Ogura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The overexpression of Stg in Ciona neural progenitors triggers precocious G2 exit and perturbs the formation of the neural tube.
source: The overexpression of Stg in these cells triggers precocious G2 exit and perturbs the formation of the neural tube (Ogura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested neural progenitors in Ciona may be regulated in a manner akin to SOPs.
source: This suggests that G2-arrested neural progenitors in Ciona may be regulated in a manner akin to SOPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of the Stg overexpression phenotype.

claim: Muscle stem cells that contribute to the growth of the zebrafish myotome arrest in G2.
source: A recent study on the muscle stem cells that contribute to the growth of the zebrafish myotome has shown that these cells arrest in G2 but utilize a different mechanism for arrest.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature (Nguyen et al., 2017).

claim: G2-arrest in zebrafish muscle stem cells is mediated by Meox1-dependent repression of Cyclin B expression.
source: G2-arrest in this context is mediated by Meox1-dependent repression of Cyclin B expression (Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Proliferating cells in the G2 phase that are subjected to DNA damaging agents stall cell cycle progression, initiate DNA repair, and rekindle the cell cycle after repair is completed.
source: Proliferating cells in the G2 phase that are subjected to DNA damaging agents stall cell cycle progression, initiate DNA repair, and rekindle the cell cycle after repair is completed (Branzei and Foiani, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Genotoxic stress leads to the activation of the phosphoinositide-3-kinase-related kinases ATR and ATM that phosphorylate and activate Checkpoint Kinases 1 and 2 (Chk1,2) respectively.
source: Genotoxic stress leads to the activation of the phosphoinositide-3-kinase-related kinases ATR and ATM that phosphorylate and activate Checkpoint Kinases 1 and 2 (Chk1,2) respectively(Kumagai et al., 2004; Chaturvedi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chk1 and Chk2 inhibit Cdc25 and arrest cell cycle progression.
source: Chk1 and Chk2, in turn, inhibit Cdc25 and arrest cell cycle progression (Xiao et al., 2003; Chaturvedi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chk1 can also stabilize the Wee/Myt kinases that phosphorylate and inhibit Cdc2/Cdk1.
source: In addition, Chk1 can also stabilize the Wee/Myt kinases that phosphorylate and inhibit Cdc2/Cdk1(O'Connell et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ATR/Chk1 can regulate cell cycle progression in cultured cells in the absence of induced DNA damage.
source: While there is evidence that ATR/Chk1 can regulate cell cycle progression in cultured cells in the absence of induced DNA damage (Sørensen et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2006) and during early embryonic development (Sibon et al., 1999; Sibon et al., 1997; Su et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2000) their roles in developmental G2 arrest have not been fully explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATR/Chk1 can regulate cell cycle progression during early embryonic development.
source: While there is evidence that ATR/Chk1 can regulate cell cycle progression in cultured cells in the absence of induced DNA damage (Sørensen et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2006) and during early embryonic development (Sibon et al., 1999; Sibon et al., 1997; Su et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2000) their roles in developmental G2 arrest have not been fully explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The roles of ATR/Chk1 in developmental G2 arrest have not been fully explored.
source: While there is evidence that ATR/Chk1 can regulate cell cycle progression in cultured cells in the absence of induced DNA damage (Sørensen et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2006) and during early embryonic development (Sibon et al., 1999; Sibon et al., 1997; Su et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2000) their roles in developmental G2 arrest have not been fully explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Tracheoblasts arrest in G2 during early larval life and rekindle a mitotic program at the onset of the pupal period.
source: It has been reported that tracheoblasts arrest in G2 during early larval life and rekindle a mitotic program at the onset of the pupal period.
evidence: This is stated as previously reported knowledge.

claim: Tracheoblasts enter larval life in G1.
source: Our efforts to determine precisely when tracheoblasts enter and exit G2 showed that the cells enter larval life in G1, transition from G1 to G2 in the first larval instar (L1) and remain in G2 till the mid third larval instar (L3), a period of ~48–56 h, whereupon they enter mitosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: Tracheoblasts transition from G1 to G2 in the first larval instar (L1).
source: Our efforts to determine precisely when tracheoblasts enter and exit G2 showed that the cells enter larval life in G1, transition from G1 to G2 in the first larval instar (L1) and remain in G2 till the mid third larval instar (L3), a period of ~48–56 h, whereupon they enter mitosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: Tracheoblasts remain in G2 till the mid third larval instar (L3).
source: Our efforts to determine precisely when tracheoblasts enter and exit G2 showed that the cells enter larval life in G1, transition from G1 to G2 in the first larval instar (L1) and remain in G2 till the mid third larval instar (L3), a period of ~48–56 h, whereupon they enter mitosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: Paused tracheoblasts express Cdc2/Cdk1.
source: Moreover, we observed that paused tracheoblasts also expressed Cdc2/Cdk1 and Cyclin B.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: Paused tracheoblasts express Cyclin B.
source: Moreover, we observed that paused tracheoblasts also expressed Cdc2/Cdk1 and Cyclin B.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: G2 arrest in tracheoblasts is not mediated via transcriptional repression of Stg or of the essential drivers for G2-M.
source: These findings alerted us to the possibility that G2 arrest is not mediated via transcriptional repression of Stg, or of the essential drivers for G2-M, and led us to investigate alternate mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that G2-arrested cells express these drivers.

claim: The G2-M transition in tracheoblasts involves the coordination of several processes including the downregulation of Chk1.
source: The findings presented here show that the G2-M transition in tracheoblasts is negatively regulated by ATR (mei-41, hereafter ATR)/Chk1 (Grapes (Grp), hereafter Chk1), that the transition involves the coordination of several processes including the downregulation of Chk1, and that arrest in G2 facilitates cellular and organ growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: The tracheal system of the Drosophila larva originates in the embryo from a pair of placodes in each segment.
source: The tracheal system of the Drosophila larva originates in the embryo from a pair of placodes in each segment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila tracheal development.

claim: Each tracheal placode undergoes branching morphogenesis to generate tracheal tubes that anastomose at stereotyped locations and generate a connected network.
source: Each placode undergoes branching morphogenesis to generate tracheal tubes that anastomose at stereotyped locations and generate a connected network.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila tracheal development.

claim: The larval tracheal system is largely comprised of cells that undergo repeated cycles of endoreplication and are post-mitotic.
source: The larval tracheal system is largely comprised of cells that undergo repeated cycles of endoreplication and are post-mitotic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila tracheal development.

claim: Imaginal tracheal progenitors are embedded in larval tracheae at stereotyped locations.
source: Embedded in larval tracheae, at stereotyped locations, are imaginal tracheal progenitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila tracheal development.

claim: Imaginal tracheal progenitors remain mitotically quiescent through larval life and proliferate and replace larval cells during metamorphosis.
source: These cells remain mitotically quiescent through larval life and proliferate and replace larval cells during metamorphosis (Pitsouli and Perrimon, 2010; Weaver and Krasnow, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The majority of the cells that populate Tr2 tracheae during larval stages are imaginal progenitors.
source: To the best of our knowledge, majority of the cells that populate Tr2 tracheae during larval stages are also imaginal progenitors (Figure 1A, shown in green)(Guha et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The cells that comprise Tr2 tracheae are mitotically competent.
source: Unlike post-mitotic larval tracheal cells, the cells that comprise Tr2 tracheae are mitotically competent, remain paused in G2 during larval life, and rekindle mitoses in the third larval instar (L3)(Guha et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2008; Djabrayan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cells that comprise Tr2 tracheae remain paused in G2 during larval life.
source: Unlike post-mitotic larval tracheal cells, the cells that comprise Tr2 tracheae are mitotically competent, remain paused in G2 during larval life, and rekindle mitoses in the third larval instar (L3)(Guha et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2008; Djabrayan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cells that comprise Tr2 tracheae rekindle mitoses in the third larval instar (L3).
source: Unlike post-mitotic larval tracheal cells, the cells that comprise Tr2 tracheae are mitotically competent, remain paused in G2 during larval life, and rekindle mitoses in the third larval instar (L3)(Guha et al., 2008; Sato et al., 2008; Djabrayan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are 16-18 cells in Tr2 DT in L1.
source: Counts of cell numbers in Tr2 DT showed that there are 16–18 cells in L1, that this number remains unchanged through 16–24 h L3, that there are 25–35 cells by 32–40 h L3 and ~250 cells at wandering L3 (WL3) (Figure 1I, n ≥ 5 tracheae per timepoint here and in all subsequent figures showing cell frequencies).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The number of cells in Tr2 DT remains unchanged through 16-24 h L3.
source: Counts of cell numbers in Tr2 DT showed that there are 16–18 cells in L1, that this number remains unchanged through 16–24 h L3, that there are 25–35 cells by 32–40 h L3 and ~250 cells at wandering L3 (WL3) (Figure 1I, n ≥ 5 tracheae per timepoint here and in all subsequent figures showing cell frequencies).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There are 25-35 cells in Tr2 DT by 32-40 h L3.
source: Counts of cell numbers in Tr2 DT showed that there are 16–18 cells in L1, that this number remains unchanged through 16–24 h L3, that there are 25–35 cells by 32–40 h L3 and ~250 cells at wandering L3 (WL3) (Figure 1I, n ≥ 5 tracheae per timepoint here and in all subsequent figures showing cell frequencies).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There are approximately 250 cells in Tr2 DT at wandering L3 (WL3).
source: Counts of cell numbers in Tr2 DT showed that there are 16–18 cells in L1, that this number remains unchanged through 16–24 h L3, that there are 25–35 cells by 32–40 h L3 and ~250 cells at wandering L3 (WL3) (Figure 1I, n ≥ 5 tracheae per timepoint here and in all subsequent figures showing cell frequencies).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1I.

claim: BrdU incorporation in Tr2 was observed in the first larval instar (L1).
source: BrdU incorporation in Tr2 was observed in the first larval instar (L1) and again at 32–40 h L3 but not in the interim period.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: BrdU incorporation in Tr2 was observed again at 32-40 h L3.
source: BrdU incorporation in Tr2 was observed in the first larval instar (L1) and again at 32–40 h L3 but not in the interim period.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: BrdU incorporation in Tr2 was not observed in the period between L1 and 32-40 h L3.
source: BrdU incorporation in Tr2 was observed in the first larval instar (L1) and again at 32–40 h L3 but not in the interim period.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations.

claim: Phospho-histone H3 labeling was detected from 32-40 h L3 onwards.
source: Phospho-histone H3 labeling was detected from 32- 40 h L3 onwards (representative images from different stages and a quantitation of pH3+ cells at these stages is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells in Tr2 DT complete S phase in L1 and remain in G2 from late L1/L2 till 24-32 h L3.
source: Based on these analyses we surmised that cells in Tr2 DT complete S phase in L1 and remain in G2 from late L1/L2 till 24–32 h L3.
evidence: This is an inference based on BrdU incorporation and pH3 labeling data.

claim: Cells in Tr2 DT are heterogeneous with respect to FUCCI reporter expression in L1.
source: We found that cells in Tr2 DT are heterogeneous with respect to reporter expression in L1 (GFP+,RFP+ and GFP+RFP+) (Figure 1B), homogeneous from L2 till early L3 (GFP+RFP+) (L2 shown Figures 1C, 0-8 h L3 not shown, 16–24 h L3 shown in Figure 1D) and heterogeneous from 32-40 hL3 onwards (GFP+, RFP+ and GFP+RFP+) (32–40 h L3 shown in Figure 1E, WL3 shown in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells in Tr2 DT are homogeneous (GFP+RFP+) from L2 till early L3.
source: We found that cells in Tr2 DT are heterogeneous with respect to reporter expression in L1 (GFP+,RFP+ and GFP+RFP+) (Figure 1B), homogeneous from L2 till early L3 (GFP+RFP+) (L2 shown Figures 1C, 0-8 h L3 not shown, 16–24 h L3 shown in Figure 1D) and heterogeneous from 32-40 hL3 onwards (GFP+, RFP+ and GFP+RFP+) (32–40 h L3 shown in Figure 1E, WL3 shown in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Cells in Tr2 DT are heterogeneous with respect to FUCCI reporter expression from 32-40 h L3 onwards.
source: We found that cells in Tr2 DT are heterogeneous with respect to reporter expression in L1 (GFP+,RFP+ and GFP+RFP+) (Figure 1B), homogeneous from L2 till early L3 (GFP+RFP+) (L2 shown Figures 1C, 0-8 h L3 not shown, 16–24 h L3 shown in Figure 1D) and heterogeneous from 32-40 hL3 onwards (GFP+, RFP+ and GFP+RFP+) (32–40 h L3 shown in Figure 1E, WL3 shown in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: The cells in Tr2 DT are all GFP+ in freshly hatched L1s.
source: Analysis of freshly hatched L1s showed that the cells in Tr2 DT are all GFP+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The DNA content of cells in L2 and early L3 was comparable to the DNA content of cells in G2 at WL3.
source: We noted that the DNA content of cells in L2 and early L3 was comparable to the DNA content of cells in G2.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Levels of Stg mRNA at L2, 0-8 h L3, 16-24 h L3 and 32-40 h L3 were comparable.
source: Levels of Stg mRNA at L2, 0–8 h L3, 16–24 h L3 and 32–40 h L3 were comparable (Figure 1I) and the level at WL3 was significantly higher than earlier stages (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The level of Stg mRNA at WL3 was significantly higher than earlier stages.
source: Levels of Stg mRNA at L2, 0–8 h L3, 16–24 h L3 and 32–40 h L3 were comparable (Figure 1I) and the level at WL3 was significantly higher than earlier stages (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Stg immunostaining revealed low levels of Stg, in both nucleus and cytosol, at L2, 0-8 h L3 and 32-40 h L3.
source: Stg immunostaining revealed low levels of Stg, in both nucleus and cytosol, at L2, 0–8 h L3 and 32–40 h L3 (Figure 1J, n = 9 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3 experiments).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Higher levels of Stg were detected at WL3 with the same spatial distribution as earlier stages.
source: We detected higher levels, with the same spatial distribution as earlier stages, at WL3 (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Tracheoblasts paused in G2 express both Stg mRNA and protein.
source: These experiments suggest that unlike SOPs, tracheoblasts paused in G2 express both Stg mRNA and protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on qPCR and immunostaining data.

claim: Both Cdc2/Cdk1 mRNA and protein were detected in paused cells.
source: Both mRNA and protein were detected in paused cells and exhibited a timecourse of expression like Stg/Stg (qPCR data and immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, qPCR as above n = 3, immunohistochemistry n = 6 tracheae per condition, n = 2 experiments).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on qPCR and immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both Cyclin B mRNA and protein were detected in paused cells.
source: Both mRNA and protein were detected in paused cells and exhibited a timecourse of expression like Stg/Stg (qPCR data and immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, qPCR as above n = 3, immunohistochemistry n = 6 tracheae per condition, n = 2 experiments).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on qPCR and immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: G2-arrested cells in Tr2 DT express all the cell cycle regulators necessary for G2-M.
source: Together, the findings suggest that G2-arrested cells in Tr2 DT express all the cell cycle regulators necessary for G2-M.
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of Stg, Cdc2/Cdk1, and Cyclin B in paused cells.

claim: The co-overexpression of Stg, Cdc2/Cdk1 and Cyclin B did not result in increased numbers of cells in L2 and early L3.
source: The co-overexpression of Stg, Cdc2/Cdk1 and Cyclin B did not result in increased numbers of cells (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1K.

claim: G2 arrest in tracheoblasts could be due to the expression of negative regulators of G2-M and/or the paucity of other positive regulators.
source: This suggestedthat G2 arrest in tracheoblasts could be due to the expression of negative regulators of G2-M and/or the paucity of other positive regulators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of overexpression to induce mitosis.

claim: The numbers of cells in Tr2 DT in Btl-ATRRNAi larvae were significantly higher than wild type by 16-24 h in L3.
source: The numbers of cells in Tr2 DT in Btl-ATRRNAi larvae were significantly higher than wild type by 16–24 h in L3 (21–26 cells compared to 16–18 cells, Figure 2A) while there was no increase in cell number in Btl-ATMRNAi expressing animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no increase in cell number in Btl-ATMRNAi expressing animals.
source: The numbers of cells in Tr2 DT in Btl-ATRRNAi larvae were significantly higher than wild type by 16–24 h in L3 (21–26 cells compared to 16–18 cells, Figure 2A) while there was no increase in cell number in Btl-ATMRNAi expressing animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ATR-Chk1 axis and not the ATM-Chk2 axis is implicated in the regulation of G2 arrest in Tr2 DT.
source: This finding implicated the ATR-Chk1 axis and not the ATM-Chk2 axis in the regulation of G2 arrest in Tr2 DT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of ATR and ATM knockdown.

claim: Anti-phospho-Chk1 (pChk1) immunostaining was high in L2 and early L3 and low at 32-40 h L3.
source: Anti-phospho-Chk1 (pChk1) immunostaining was high in L2 and early L3 and low at 32–40 h L3 (Figure 2B, n = 6–8 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3) and subsequent stages (WL3, data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chk1 phosphorylation is ATR-dependent.
source: We stained for pChk1 in Btl-ATRRNAi animals and found no detectable signal indicating that Chk1 phosphorylation is indeed ATR-dependent (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of cells in Tr2 DT in Btl-Chk1RNAi larvae is higher by 16-24 h in L3 (40-50 cells).
source: Cell counts of Btl-Chk1RNAi larvae showed that the number of cells in in Tr2 DT is higher by 16–24 h in L3 (40–50 cells, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2D.

claim: pH3+ mitotic figures were observed in Btl-ATRRNAi at 16-24 h L3.
source: We observed pH3+ mitotic figures in Btl-ATRRNAi at 16–24 h and in Btl-Chk1RNAi expressing animals at 0–8 h L3 and 16–24 h L3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 2E.

claim: pH3+ mitotic figures were observed in Btl-Chk1RNAi expressing animals at 0-8 h L3 and 16-24 h L3.
source: We observed pH3+ mitotic figures in Btl-ATRRNAi at 16–24 h and in Btl-Chk1RNAi expressing animals at 0–8 h L3 and 16–24 h L3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The overexpression of Chk1 inhibited mitotic entry at 32-40 h L3.
source: The overexpression of Chk1 under Btl control (Btl-Chk1) inhibited mitotic entry at 32–40 h L3 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ATR/Chk1 are negative regulators of G2-M in tracheoblasts.
source: Based on these findings we conclude that ATR/Chk1 are negative regulators of G2-M in tracheoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing that loss of ATR/Chk1 leads to precocious mitosis and overexpression inhibits mitosis.

claim: The numbers of cells in Tr2 DT at WL3 in ATR/Chk1-deficient animals were significantly lower than in wild type.
source: Despite precocious mitotic entry in ATR/Chk1-deficient animals, the numbers of cells in Tr2 DT at WL3 in these animals were significantly lower than in wild type (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figures 2A and 2D.

claim: Expression of Chk1RNAi from embryonic stages till WL3 led to a reduction in the numbers of cells at WL3.
source: The expression of Chk1RNAi from embryonic stages (animals raised at 29°C till WL3 to inactivate Gal-80) led to a reduction in the numbers of cells at WL3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of Chk1RNAi from embryonic stages till 24 h L3 did not lead to a reduction in the numbers of cells in Tr2 DT at WL3.
source: However, expression of Chk1RNAi from embryonic stages till 24 h L3 (animals grown at 29°C from embryonic stages to 24 h L3 and shifted to 18°C from 24 h L3 to WL3) did not lead to a reduction in the numbers of cells in Tr2 DT at WL3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Chk1 has a role in tracheoblasts post mitotic entry.
source: This suggests that in addition to regulating G2-M, Chk1 has a role in tracheoblasts post mitotic entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditional knockdown experiments.

claim: The frequencies of BrdU+ cells were comparable in Btl-Chk1RNAi and wild type in late L3.
source: The frequencies of BrdU+ cells were comparable in Btl-Chk1RNAi and wild type but the frequency of pH3+ cells was significantly higher in Btl-Chk1RNAi (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The frequency of pH3+ cells was significantly higher in Btl-Chk1RNAi than wild type in late L3.
source: The frequencies of BrdU+ cells were comparable in Btl-Chk1RNAi and wild type but the frequency of pH3+ cells was significantly higher in Btl-Chk1RNAi (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The frequencies of activated Caspase3+ cells were comparable in Btl-Chk1RNAi and wild type.
source: The frequencies of activated Caspase3+ cells were comparable in Btl-Chk1RNAi and wild type (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cells lacking Chk1 divide more slowly on account of a prolonged M phase.
source: Together, reduced numbers of cells in Btl-Chk1RNAi in late L3 and increased frequency of pH3+ cells in these animals at the same stage suggests that cells lacking Chk1 divide more slowly on account of a prolonged M phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of reduced cell numbers and increased pH3+ frequency.

claim: ATR-Chk1 has a role in the regulation of the mitotic spindle during cytokinesis.
source: These data are consistent with a previously described role for ATR-Chk1 in the regulation of the mitotic spindle during cytokinesis (Gruber et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in Tr2 DT enter G2 late in L1/early L2 and remain in G2 till 24-32 h L3.
source: Cells in Tr2 DT enter G2 late in L1/early L2 and remain in G2 till 24–32 h L3.
evidence: This is a summary of findings reported earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The loss of ATR/Chk1 results in mitotic entry in early L3, approximately 24-32 h earlier than normal.
source: The loss of ATR/Chk1 results in mitotic entry in early L3, ~24–32 h earlier than normal.
evidence: This is a summary of findings reported earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Cdc2AF induction in L2 did not lead to an increase in cell number.
source: We observed that Cdc2AF induction in L2 did not lead to an increase in cell number but induction at 0–8 h L3 and 32–40 h L3 did (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cdc2AF induction at 0-8 h L3 and 32-40 h L3 led to an increase in cell number.
source: We observed that Cdc2AF induction in L2 did not lead to an increase in cell number but induction at 0–8 h L3 and 32–40 h L3 did (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cdc2 was expressed in L2 and L3 and upregulated post heat shock.
source: The staining showed that Cdc2 was expressed in L2 and L3 and upregulated post heat shock (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The induction of Cdc2AF is unable to induce proliferation in L2 but is able to at subsequent stages.
source: We conclude that the induction of Cdc2AF is unable to induce proliferation in L2 but is able to at subsequent stages.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Co-overexpression of Cdc2AF and Cyclin B in L2 was unable to induce division.
source: We also co-overexpressed Cdc2AF and Cyclin B in L2 and found that this combination was also unable to induce division in L2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The inability of Cdc2AF to induce mitoses in L2 implicates an ATR-Chk1-independent process in the regulation of G2 arrest in L2.
source: The inability of Cdc2AF to induce mitoses in L2 was consistent with the lack of proliferation in ATRRNAi/Chk1RNAi at this stage and implicated an ATR-Chk1-independent process in the regulation of G2 arrest in L2 (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Levels of pChk1 are high in L2 and early L3 and diminished at 32-40 hr L3 upon mitotic entry.
source: Our analysis of Tr2 DT has shown that Chk1 is phosphorylated in an ATR-dependent manner (Figure 2) and that levels of pChk1 are high in L2 and early L3 and diminished at 32–40 hr L3 upon mitotic entry (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of findings reported earlier in the manuscript.

claim: No gamma-H2AX staining was detected in Tr2 DT in L2.
source: We detected no gamma-H2AX staining in Tr2 DT in L2 and sporadic staining in WL3 (Figure 5A–B, early L3 not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: Sporadic gamma-H2AX staining was detected in Tr2 DT in WL3.
source: We detected no gamma-H2AX staining in Tr2 DT in L2 and sporadic staining in WL3 (Figure 5A–B, early L3 not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: No gamma-H2AX was detected in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals in L2.
source: We also examined gamma-H2AX levels in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals to see if the levels were elevated. Here again, we detected no gamma-H2AX in L2 and some labeling, at levels comparable to wild type, at WL3 (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: Some gamma-H2AX labeling was detected in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals at WL3, at levels comparable to wild type.
source: We also examined gamma-H2AX levels in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals to see if the levels were elevated. Here again, we detected no gamma-H2AX in L2 and some labeling, at levels comparable to wild type, at WL3 (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on immunostaining shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: There is no evidence for double-strand breaks in DNA in cells paused in G2.
source: Thus, we found no evidence for double-strand breaks in DNA in cells paused in G2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of gamma-H2AX staining.

claim: Levels of ATR expression were slightly increased at 0-8 h L3 with respect to expression at L2.
source: With respect to expression at L2, levels of ATR expression were slightly increased at 0–8 h L3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The levels of Chk1 mRNA were approximately 5 fold higher at both L2 and 0-8 h L3 in comparison to 32-40 h L3.
source: Interestingly, the levels of Chk1 mRNA were ~5 fold higher at both L2 and 0–8 h L3 in comparison to 32–40 h L3 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The high levels of pChk1 in Tr2 DT in L2 and early L3 could be regulated at a transcriptional level via the regulation of Chk1 expression.
source: This suggests that the high levels of pChk1 in Tr2 DT in L2 and early L3 could be regulated at a transcriptional level via the regulation of Chk1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qPCR data showing higher Chk1 mRNA levels in arrested cells.

claim: Most of the growth of Tr2 DT occurs from the time the animals enter L2 till mid-L3.
source: Measurements of the length and width of Tr2 DT at different larval stages showed that most of the growth of this segment occurs from the time the animals enter L2 till mid-L3 (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements shown in Figures 6A-B.

claim: Tr2 DT grows in length by 268 ± 32% during the L2 to mid-L3 period.
source: During this period, Tr2 DT grows in length by 268 ± 32% (n = 6 tracheae) and in width by 247 ± 19% (n = 12 tracheae).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements.

claim: Tr2 DT grows in width by 247 ± 19% during the L2 to mid-L3 period.
source: During this period, Tr2 DT grows in length by 268 ± 32% (n = 6 tracheae) and in width by 247 ± 19% (n = 12 tracheae).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements.

claim: Between L2 and 24-32 h L3, cells in Tr2 DT virtually doubled in size (cellular area increased by 112 ± 37%).
source: Between L2 and 24–32 h L3, cells virtually doubled in size (cellular area increased by 112 ± 37% (n = 15)) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Maximal growth of Tr2 DT and the tracheoblasts that comprise it occurs in the period when the tracheoblasts are paused in G2.
source: Thus, analysis of the growth trajectory of Tr2 DT, and the tracheoblasts that comprise it,showed that maximal growth occurs in the period when the tracheoblasts are paused in G2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of growth and G2 arrest.

claim: The arrest in G2 may facilitate the growth of cells and the tracheal branches they comprise.
source: This raised the possibility that the arrest in G2 facilitates the growth of cells and the tracheal branches they comprise.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the correlation between G2 arrest and growth.

claim: The growth of Tr2 DT was significantly reduced in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals at 32-40 hr L3 in comparison to wild type.
source: Measurements of length and width of Tr2 DT in Btl- Chk1RNAi animals at 32–40 hr L3 showed that the growth was significantly reduced in comparison to wild type (Figure 6D, both average length and width are statistically different p<0.05, see Source data file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Tr2 DT segments were significantly larger in animals overexpressing Chk1.
source: Conversely, the measurements of length and width of Tr2 DT in animals overexpressing Chk1 showed thatTr2 DT segments were significantly larger in this background (Figure 6D, p<0.05, both average length and width are statistically different p<0.05, see Source data file 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The sizes of trachea in wild type, Btl-Chk1RNAi and Btl-Chk1 animals at 0-8 h L3 are comparable.
source: We then compared the sizes of trachea in wild type, Btl- Chk1RNAi and Btl-Chk1 animals at 0–8 h L3 and found that they are comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATR/Chk1-dependent G2 arrest facilitates cellular and organ growth in Tr2.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that ATR/Chk1-dependent G2 arrest facilitates cellular and organ growth in Tr2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing that loss of Chk1 reduces growth and overexpression increases growth.

claim: Tr2 tracheoblasts remain arrested in G2 for approximately 48-56 h during larval life during which the cells and the tracheae they comprise grow in size.
source: We show that Tr2 tracheoblasts remain arrested in G2 for ~48–56 h during larval life during which the cells and the tracheae they comprise grow in size.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Tracheoblasts paused in G2 express both the essential drivers for G2-M like Cdc2/Cdk1, Cyclin B and Stg, and negative regulators of G2-M like ATR and Chk1.
source: Our findings are that tracheoblasts paused in G2 express both the essential drivers for G2-M like Cdc2/Cdk1, Cyclin B and Stg, and negative regulators of G2-M like ATR and Chk1, and that the G2-M transition in these cells involves the coordination of several genetically distinguishable processes including the downregulation of Chk1.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Arrest in G2 is necessary for growth of tracheoblasts and the tracheae they comprise.
source: Our analysis also reveals that arrest in G2 is necessary for growth of tracheoblasts and the tracheae they comprise.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: ATR is recruited to stalled/collapsed replication forks during DNA replication and to double-strand DNA breaks that occur upon exposure DNA damaging agents or during recombination.
source: In these contexts, ATR is recruited to stalled/collapsed replication forks during DNA replication and to double-strand DNA breaks that occur upon exposure DNA damaging agents or during recombination (Kumagai et al., 2004; Blythe and Wieschaus, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recruitment of ATR leads to the phosphorylation and activation of Chk1 and to the inhibition of Cdc2/Cdk1 activity.
source: Recruitment of ATR leads in turn to the phosphorylation and activation of Chk1 and to the inhibition of Cdc2/Cdk1 activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ATR-Chk1 pathway.

claim: The inhibition of ATR/Chk1 has been shown to hinder completion of DNA replication and DNA repair and result in aberrant mitoses.
source: The inhibition of ATR/Chk1 has been shown to hinder completion of DNA replication and DNA repair and result in aberrant mitoses; ATR/Chk1 mutant animals are embryonic lethal (Liu et al., 2000; Sibon et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATR/Chk1 mutant animals are embryonic lethal.
source: The inhibition of ATR/Chk1 has been shown to hinder completion of DNA replication and DNA repair and result in aberrant mitoses; ATR/Chk1 mutant animals are embryonic lethal (Liu et al., 2000; Sibon et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATR/Chk1 act to arrest cells in G2 in the context of tracheoblasts.
source: In the context of tracheoblasts, we find that ATR/Chk1 act to arrest cells in G2.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: There is no evidence for any DNA damage in cells in which Chk1 is active.
source: But unlike in other contexts, we find no evidence for any DNA damage in cells in which Chk1 is active nor any increase in DNA damage upon reduction of Chk1 levels and the induction of precocious mitoses.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on gamma-H2AX staining.

claim: There is no increase in DNA damage upon reduction of Chk1 levels and the induction of precocious mitoses.
source: But unlike in other contexts, we find no evidence for any DNA damage in cells in which Chk1 is active nor any increase in DNA damage upon reduction of Chk1 levels and the induction of precocious mitoses.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on gamma-H2AX staining.

claim: It appears unlikely that the activation of ATR/Chk1 in Tr2 DT is the outcome of the activation of the canonical DNA damage checkpoint.
source: Thus, it appears unlikely that the activation of ATR/Chk1 in Tr2 DT is the outcome of the activation of the canonical DNA damage checkpoint.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of DNA damage markers.

claim: Increased expression of Chk1 mRNA could contribute toward increased levels of phosphorylated Chk1 and to G2 arrest.
source: Increased expression of Chk1 mRNA could contribute toward increased levels of phosphorylated Chk1 and to G2 arrest.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the qPCR data.

claim: Wee/Myt1 do not contribute toward G2 arrest in tracheoblasts.
source: We find that the expression of WeeRNAi and Myt1RNAi does not recapitulate the Chk1RNAi phenotype (data not shown). This suggests that Wee/Myt1 do not contribute toward G2 arrest in tracheoblasts and that Chk1 acts via the inhibition of Stg.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phenotype with Wee/Myt1 knockdown.

claim: Chk1 acts via the inhibition of Stg in tracheoblasts.
source: We find that the expression of WeeRNAi and Myt1RNAi does not recapitulate the Chk1RNAi phenotype (data not shown). This suggests that Wee/Myt1 do not contribute toward G2 arrest in tracheoblasts and that Chk1 acts via the inhibition of Stg.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phenotype with Wee/Myt1 knockdown.

claim: The precocious proliferation in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals is dependent on Stg.
source: We have examined if the precocious proliferation in Btl-Chk1RNAi animals is dependent on Stg. Counts of cell numbers in Tr2 DT in Btl-Chk1RNAiStgRNAi animals showed that there was no increase at 16–24 h L3 or at 32–40 h L3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding reported based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mechanism for arrest in L2 is likely to be independent of ATR/Chk1.
source: This shows that the mechanism for arrest in L2 is likely to be independent of ATR/Chk1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inability of Cdc2AF to induce mitosis in L2.

claim: The inhibition of mitochondrial fission in actively proliferating cells leads to arrest in G2.
source: Several studies have shown that the inhibition of mitochondrial fission in actively proliferating cells leads to arrest in G2 (Westrate et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in which mitochondrial fission was inhibited were unresponsive to expression of Cdc2AF.
source: Importantly, a recent study has shown that cells in which mitochondrial fission was inhibited were also unresponsive to expression of Cdc2AF(Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The tracheal epithelium grows in volume approximately 13 fold in the L2-32-40 h L3 interval.
source: Based on the quantitation of tracheal size (Figure 6), we estimate that the tracheal epithelium, and at least some of the tracheoblasts that comprise it, grow in volume ~13 fold in the L2-32-40 h L3 interval.
evidence: This is an estimate based on measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Histoblasts arrested in G2 grow approximately 60 fold in volume.
source: Histoblasts arrested in G2 grow ~60 fold in volume (Ninov et al., 2009) and Drosophila spermatocytes arrested in pre-meiotic G2 arrest grow ~25 fold in volume (Ueishi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila spermatocytes arrested in pre-meiotic G2 arrest grow approximately 25 fold in volume.
source: Histoblasts arrested in G2 grow ~60 fold in volume (Ninov et al., 2009) and Drosophila spermatocytes arrested in pre-meiotic G2 arrest grow ~25 fold in volume (Ueishi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Abrogating G2 arrest in developing tracheoblasts via knockdown of ATR/Chk1 diminishes cellular and organ growth.
source: We find that abrogating G2 arrest in developing tracheoblasts via knockdown of ATR/Chk1 diminishes cellular and organ growth.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Prolonging G2 arrest leads to increased growth.
source: Conversely, prolonging G2 arrest leads to increased growth.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Arrest in G2 may facilitate cellular growth.
source: It is plausible that arrest in G2 facilitates cellular growth.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cellular growth may drive hypertrophic organ growth and facilitate rapid proliferation subsequently.
source: This cellular growth may drive hypertrophic organ growth as we show here and facilitate rapid proliferation subsequently.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Hypertrophic growth in the vertebrate kidney is associated with cells in G1 arrest.
source: Analysis of the mechanisms underlying hypertrophic growth in the vertebrate kidney (Shankland and Wolf, 2000) and heart (Braun-Dullaeus et al., 1999) has shown that it is associated with cells in G1 arrest.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hypertrophic growth in the vertebrate heart is associated with cells in G1 arrest.
source: Analysis of the mechanisms underlying hypertrophic growth in the vertebrate kidney (Shankland and Wolf, 2000) and heart (Braun-Dullaeus et al., 1999) has shown that it is associated with cells in G1 arrest.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G2-arrested cells may be relevant to hypertrophic organ growth and pathogenesis.
source: The findings presented here suggest that G2-arrested cells may also be relevant to hypertrophic organ growth and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Hypertrophic cellular growth in G1-arrested cells has been shown to be dependent on the juxtaposition of cell cycle activators and inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, hypertrophic cellular growth in G1-arrested cells referred to above has been shown to be dependent on the juxtaposition of cell cycle activators and inhibitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hypertrophic growth mechanisms.

claim: In the context of glomerular cell hypertrophy associated with diabetic nephropathy, elevated glucose levels induced quiescent cells to enter G1 while Angiotensin II and TGF-Beta signaling elevated levels of CDK inhibitors that prevented entry into S phase.
source: In the context of glomerular cell hypertrophy associated with diabetic nephropathy, elevated glucose levels induced quiescent cells to enter G1 while Angiotensin II and TGF-Beta signaling elevated levels of CDK inhibitors that prevented entry into S phase (Fujita et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The negative regulation of cell cycle progression in cells that are mitotically active may be necessary for the hypertrophic growth of G2-arrested cells.
source: The negative regulation of cell cycle progression in cells that are mitotically active may be necessary for the hypertrophic growth of G2-arrested cells as well.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by analogy to G1-arrested cells.
